concepts.title: net/http Fundamentals: Handlers and Routing
concepts.description: The entire net/http server story rests on one tiny interface, http.Handler, and one adapter type, http.HandlerFunc, that lets an ordinary function satisfy it -- understanding both, plus how http.ServeMux matches a request to a handler, is what everything else in building an HTTP service in Go is built on top of.
learningObjectives: Explain the http.Handler interface's single method and what ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) is responsible for doing.
Explain what http.HandlerFunc is and why it lets an ordinary function value satisfy the Handler interface without defining a new named type.
Register routes on an http.ServeMux and start a server with http.ListenAndServe, and explain the role of http.DefaultServeMux.
Use Go 1.22+ enhanced ServeMux patterns (HTTP method prefixes and {wildcard} path segments) to route requests without a third-party router.
Explain why calling w.Write before setting a header, or calling w.WriteHeader more than once, produces bugs that don't show up as compile errors.

sections.heading: http.Handler: One Method, the Same Philosophy as io.Reader
http.HandlerFunc: Adapting a Plain Function Into a Handler
sections.body:
Defining a whole named struct type with a `ServeHTTP` method, as above, is overkill for the very common case of a handler that's really just one function with no state of its own. `http.HandlerFunc` is a small, elegant adapter type that solves this:

```go
type HandlerFunc func(ResponseWriter, *Request)

func (f HandlerFunc) ServeHTTP(w ResponseWriter, r *Request) {
	f(w, r)
}
```

`HandlerFunc` is a **named function type** -- any value with the underlying signature `func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)` can be converted to it, and once converted, it has a `ServeHTTP` method (defined right there in the standard library) that simply calls the underlying function itself. This is the mechanism that lets you write handlers as plain functions:

```go
func helloHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	fmt.Fprintln(w, "Hello from a plain function!")
}

http.Handle("/hello", http.HandlerFunc(helloHandler))   // explicit conversion, then it satisfies Handler
```

Note the explicit conversion, `http.HandlerFunc(helloHandler)` -- a bare function value `helloHandler` does **not** itself have a `ServeHTTP` method; only the converted `HandlerFunc` value does. In practice, you'll far more often see `http.HandleFunc("/hello", helloHandler)` (note: `HandleFunc`, not `Handle`) -- a convenience function that performs exactly this `HandlerFunc(...)` conversion for you internally before registering the route, which is why it accepts a plain function directly while `http.Handle` requires something that's already an `http.Handler`.

sections.heading: Routing With ServeMux, and Go 1.22's Method and Wildcard Patterns
sections.body:
An `http.ServeMux` is an HTTP request multiplexer: you register patterns against handlers, and it picks the right handler for each incoming request based on the request's URL path (and, since Go 1.22, its method too):

```go
mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.HandleFunc("/", homeHandler)
mux.HandleFunc("/about", aboutHandler)
http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux)
```

`http.ListenAndServe(addr, handler)` starts a blocking TCP listener on `addr` and dispatches every incoming request to `handler`'s `ServeHTTP` method -- passing `nil` instead of an explicit mux uses `http.DefaultServeMux`, a single shared, package-level `ServeMux` that `http.HandleFunc` (the package-level function, not the method on your own mux) registers routes onto implicitly. Using the package-level default is fine for a quick script, but explicitly creating your own `http.NewServeMux()` is generally preferred in real services, since a shared global mux makes it easy for unrelated packages (including third-party ones, if any register handlers on `http.DefaultServeMux` themselves) to silently collide on route registration.

**Go 1.22** substantially upgraded what a `ServeMux` pattern can express, without needing a third-party router at all. Patterns can now be prefixed with an HTTP method, and path segments can contain named wildcards:

```go
mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", getUserHandler)
mux.HandleFunc("DELETE /users/{id}", deleteUserHandler)

func getUserHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	id := r.PathValue("id")   // the actual path segment matched by {id}
	fmt.Fprintf(w, "fetching user %s", id)
}
```

`"GET /users/{id}"` only matches GET requests to a path shaped like `/users/anything`; a DELETE request to the exact same path is routed to the separate `"DELETE /users/{id}"` registration instead, with no manual `if r.Method == "GET"` branching required inside either handler. `r.PathValue("id")` retrieves whatever the `{id}` segment actually matched for that specific request. Before Go 1.22, achieving either of these (method-specific routing, path parameters) with only the standard library meant manually inspecting `r.Method` and parsing `r.URL.Path` yourself, which is exactly why so many pre-1.22 Go services reached for a third-party router (like gorilla/mux or chi) purely for this capability -- a need that's now substantially reduced.

sections.heading: ResponseWriter: A Write-Once Status Line, and Why Order Matters

examples.title: A Struct-Based Handler and a Minimal Server
examples.explanation: `greeter` satisfies `http.Handler` purely by having a `ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)` method -- there's no declaration anywhere stating that it implements `Handler`; the compiler verifies this structurally, at the point `mux.Handle("/hello", greeter{...})` is called, since `Handle`'s second parameter is typed as `http.Handler`. Because `greeter` carries its own `name` field, each instance can be configured differently at construction time (`greeter{name: "Gopher"}` here), which a bare function-based handler couldn't do without reaching for a closure or package-level variable instead -- this is exactly the situation where a struct-based handler earns its extra verbosity over a plain `HandlerFunc`.

examples.title: HandlerFunc and the http.HandleFunc Convenience
examples.explanation: `helloHandler` is an ordinary function with signature `func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)` -- on its own, it has no methods and does not satisfy `http.Handler`. `mux.HandleFunc("/hello", helloHandler)` accepts exactly this plain function signature (not an `http.Handler`) and performs the `http.HandlerFunc(helloHandler)` conversion internally before storing it, which is precisely why `HandleFunc` exists as a distinct method alongside `Handle`: `Handle` requires you to already have an `http.Handler` (like the `greeter` struct in the previous example); `HandleFunc` accepts a bare function and does the wrapping for you, which is why nearly all simple, stateless handlers in real Go code are registered with `HandleFunc` rather than manually writing `mux.Handle("/hello", http.HandlerFunc(helloHandler))`.

examples.title: Go 1.22 Method-Specific and Wildcard Routing
examples.explanation: The two registrations share the exact same path shape, `/users/{id}`, but are distinguished entirely by their leading HTTP method prefix -- `GET /users/{id}` and `DELETE /users/{id}` are two independent, non-overlapping route registrations, and ServeMux itself routes an incoming DELETE request to the second handler and a GET request to the first, with neither handler ever needing to inspect `r.Method` manually. `r.PathValue("id")` reads whichever concrete path segment matched the named `{id}` wildcard for that specific request -- a request to `/users/42` gives `id == "42"` regardless of which of the two method-specific handlers actually receives it. Before Go 1.22, expressing this exact routing shape with only the standard library would have required a single handler registered on the bare `/users/` prefix, manually splitting `r.URL.Path` to extract the id, and manually branching on `r.Method` inside that one handler's body.

misconceptions.description: Any function with the signature func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) automatically satisfies the http.Handler interface, with no conversion needed, the same way any type with a matching method automatically satisfies an interface.
misconceptions.clarification: Interface satisfaction in Go is based on methods, not on bare function values -- a plain function of that signature has no methods at all, and therefore does not itself satisfy http.Handler, which requires a ServeHTTP method. What actually satisfies Handler is http.HandlerFunc, a named function type with exactly that underlying signature, which the standard library gives a ServeHTTP method that simply calls the function itself. Passing a plain function where an http.Handler is expected requires an explicit conversion, http.HandlerFunc(yourFunc) -- which is exactly what the http.HandleFunc registration helper (and mux.HandleFunc) perform internally on your behalf, letting you write a plain function at the call site without writing that conversion out by hand every time.

misconceptions.description: Calling w.WriteHeader(500) after the handler has already written some body content with w.Write or fmt.Fprintln will correctly change the status code the client receives to 500.
misconceptions.clarification: The HTTP status line and headers must be sent to the client before any body bytes, and http.ResponseWriter enforces this by locking in the status code the moment it's first determined -- either by an explicit WriteHeader call, or implicitly, as 200 OK, the instant the first Write happens without one. Any WriteHeader call after that point has no effect on what the client receives (the response is already committed with whatever status was locked in first); it merely logs a 'superfluous response.WriteHeader call' warning on the server side. Avoiding this requires deciding on the final status code before writing any body content, not attempting to retroactively correct it afterward.

exercises.prompt: What HTTP status code does the client actually receive from this handler, and why, given that somethingWentWrong() returns true?
hints: The very first line calls fmt.Fprintln(w, ...), which writes body bytes through w.Write internally -- what does the FIRST Write call do if WriteHeader hasn't been explicitly called yet?
Once a status code is sent to the client -- explicitly or implicitly -- can a later WriteHeader call actually change it?
Trace exactly which line first sends the status line, and note that everything after that point is only adding to an already-committed response.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The client receives HTTP 200 OK, not 500. The first fmt.Fprintln call writes body bytes before any explicit WriteHeader call, which implicitly sends a 200 OK status immediately. The later w.WriteHeader(http.StatusInternalServerError) call has no effect on the already-sent status -- it only logs a 'superfluous WriteHeader call' warning on the server. The client sees a 200 response body containing both 'Report starting...' and 'An error occurred.'
exercises.solutionExplanation: `fmt.Fprintln(w, "Report starting...")` calls w.Write under the hood, and because no WriteHeader call has happened yet at that point, Write implicitly sends `http.StatusOK` (200) as the status code before writing the body bytes -- this happens on the very first line, unconditionally, regardless of whether somethingWentWrong() later returns true. By the time the code reaches `w.WriteHeader(http.StatusInternalServerError)`, the status is already committed and sent; that call is now a no-op as far as the client is concerned (aside from a server-side log warning), and execution continues to print 'An error occurred.' as more body content appended after the already-sent 200 status. The client therefore receives a 200 OK response whose body happens to contain text that reads like an error, which is a genuinely misleading outcome for any caller checking the status code programmatically rather than reading the body text.

exercises.prompt: This route is meant to allow only GET requests to fetch an item by id, but a DELETE request to the same path unexpectedly also matches and runs the same handler, which was never written to check the method at all. Find and fix the bug.
hints: The registered pattern, "/items/{id}", has no HTTP method prefix at all -- what requests does a ServeMux pattern with no method prefix match?
Go 1.22+ ServeMux patterns can be prefixed with a specific HTTP method, like "GET /items/{id}", to restrict matching to only that method.

Add the "GET " prefix to the pattern so only GET requests reach this handler; a DELETE (or any other method) to the same path would then fall through to any other registered pattern, or to a 404/405 if none matches.
exercises.solutionExplanation: A ServeMux pattern with no method prefix, like the original "/items/{id}", matches a request to that path regardless of its HTTP method -- GET, DELETE, POST, or anything else -- which is exactly why a DELETE request was silently routed to a handler that was only ever written with GET semantics in mind, running the same 'fetching item' logic for what should have been an entirely different operation. The fix adds an explicit method prefix, "GET /items/{id}", which is one of Go 1.22's ServeMux enhancements: the pattern now only matches requests whose method is exactly GET. A DELETE request to the same path no longer matches this registration at all -- it would need its own separate "DELETE /items/{id}" registration to be handled deliberately, or otherwise fall through to ServeMux's default 404 (or a 405 Method Not Allowed in cases where the path matches some registered pattern but no method-specific variant does).

assessments.prompt: Why does http.HandleFunc accept a plain function of type func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) directly, while http.Handle requires an argument that already satisfies http.Handler?
options: http.HandleFunc and http.Handle are actually interchangeable aliases for the exact same function with no real difference.

http.HandleFunc internally converts its function argument to the http.HandlerFunc type, which has a ServeHTTP method that calls the original function -- http.Handle has no such conversion step and requires the argument to already be a Handler.
http.Handle only works with struct-based handlers, never with functions, due to a limitation in how interfaces are implemented in Go.
http.HandleFunc registers the route but never actually calls the provided function when a request arrives; it exists only for documentation purposes.
assessments.explanation: http.HandleFunc's entire purpose is to bridge the gap between 'I have a plain function with the right signature' and 'net/http needs something with a ServeHTTP method' -- it does this by wrapping the function argument in an http.HandlerFunc value before registering it, since http.HandlerFunc is a named function type with a ServeHTTP method defined on it that simply invokes the underlying function. http.Handle, by contrast, expects you to already be passing something typed as http.Handler, with no such wrapping performed for you -- passing a bare function to Handle would be a compile error unless you performed the http.HandlerFunc(...) conversion yourself first. Option A is wrong -- they have genuinely different parameter types and behavior. Option C is wrong -- Handle works perfectly well with any http.Handler, struct-based or otherwise; the distinction is about what conversion happens automatically, not what kinds of handlers are supported. Option D is wrong -- HandleFunc's registered function absolutely is called on matching requests, exactly like any other registered handler.

assessments.prompt: Explain how net/http's Handler interface and HandlerFunc adapter reflect the same 'small interfaces over large frameworks' philosophy introduced with io.Reader, and why that design choice matters specifically for the middleware pattern covered later in this module.
assessments.modelAnswer: http.Handler is deliberately as small as an interface can be -- a single method, ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, *Request), with no required base class, no lifecycle methods to override, and no explicit declaration tying a given type to the interface. Just like io.Reader's single Read method lets an enormous range of unrelated types (files, network connections, in-memory buffers) all work with generic code like io.Copy without any of them needing to know io.Reader exists, http.Handler's single method lets anything -- a plain function wrapped via HandlerFunc, a struct carrying its own configuration and a ServeHTTP method, a router, a caching layer -- be treated identically by anything that only needs to call ServeHTTP on it, including net/http's own server loop, which has no idea what concrete type it's actually holding. HandlerFunc's role is to make this small interface friction-free for the extremely common case where a handler doesn't need to carry any state at all: rather than requiring every handler author to define a named struct type and a method just to satisfy one interface, HandlerFunc lets a plain function value be converted, with a single explicit conversion, into something that already has the required ServeHTTP method built in by the standard library. This matters enormously for middleware, covered later in this module, because middleware in Go is fundamentally a function that accepts a Handler and returns a new Handler wrapping it -- and because Handler is such a minimal, uniform interface, a middleware function doesn't need to know or care whether the Handler it's wrapping is a plain HandlerFunc-adapted function, a struct-based handler, or even another layer of middleware wrapping something else underneath; it only ever needs to call that one ServeHTTP method (or, more commonly at the source level, the equivalent) on whatever it was handed. If Handler required multiple methods, or if handlers needed to inherit from some base implementation, composing arbitrary chains of middleware around arbitrary handlers -- the entire mechanism the next concept explores -- would be dramatically more constrained and far less uniform than it is.

concepts.title: Encoding and Decoding JSON
concepts.description: encoding/json's Decoder and Encoder types stream JSON directly to and from an io.Reader/io.Writer -- exactly the kind of composition small interfaces enable -- and struct tags control precisely how Go field names map onto JSON keys, which matters enormously once you're reading untrusted request bodies and writing response bodies for real clients.
learningObjectives: Decode a JSON request body into a Go struct using json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode, and explain why streaming decode is preferable to reading the whole body into memory first.
Use struct tags (json:"name", omitempty, json:"-") to control which fields are included in encoded JSON and under what key names.
Encode a Go value to a JSON response with json.NewEncoder(w).Encode, and set the Content-Type header before writing any body content.
Distinguish the different kinds of decode errors (malformed syntax, wrong value type, empty body) and respond with an appropriate HTTP status code for each rather than a generic failure.
Explain what happens to unexported struct fields and to JSON fields with no matching struct field during decode and encode.

sections.heading: Decoding a Request Body: Decoder Over a Reader, Not Unmarshal Over Bytes
Struct Tags: Field Names, omitempty, and Exported-Only Visibility
sections.body:
By default, encoding/json includes every **exported** field of a struct in the encoded JSON, using the Go field's own name, exactly as written, as the JSON key -- `Name string` becomes `"Name": ...` with no tag needed at all to be included. A `json:"..."` struct tag lets you override that default in three common ways:

```go
type User struct {
	Name     string `json:"name"`              // renames the JSON key to lowercase "name"
	Nickname string `json:"nickname,omitempty"`  // omitted from output entirely if Nickname == ""
	password string `json:"-"`                   // unexported anyway -- always excluded, tag or not
	Internal string `json:"-"`                   // exported, but explicitly excluded via "-"
}
```

`omitempty` drops the field from the encoded JSON entirely when its value is the zero value for its type (empty string, 0, nil, false, an empty slice/map) -- useful for optional fields where you'd rather the client see no key at all than an explicit `null` or `0`. `json:"-"` unconditionally excludes a field from both encoding and decoding, regardless of its value -- the standard way to mark a field as deliberately internal-only even though it's exported (and therefore would otherwise be included by default).

This directly reuses the exported/unexported rule from the Packages concept: **unexported fields (lowercase first letter) are always excluded from JSON encoding and decoding, with no way to opt them back in via a tag** -- encoding/json, running from another package's perspective (which is effectively what it is, being generic reflection-based code with no special access), simply cannot see or set them, the same hard compiler-enforced boundary that applies to any other package. A frequent beginner mistake is defining an entire request struct with lowercase field names, expecting the tag alone to control inclusion, and then finding every field silently comes back empty after decoding -- because the tag on an unexported field has no effect at all; the field was never reachable in the first place.

sections.heading: Encoding a Response, and the Header-Before-Body Rule Again
Handling Decode Errors as Distinct, Actionable Cases
sections.body:
A `Decode` call can fail for meaningfully different reasons, and collapsing all of them into one generic 'bad request' response (or, worse, ignoring the error and proceeding with a zero-valued struct) throws away information a client could actually use to fix their request:

- **Malformed JSON syntax** -- unbalanced braces, a trailing comma, unquoted keys -- returns a `*json.SyntaxError`.
- **A JSON value that doesn't match the target field's Go type** -- a JSON string where the struct expects a number, for instance -- returns a `*json.UnmarshalTypeError`, which (unlike a syntax error) also tells you exactly which field and offset triggered it.
- **A genuinely empty request body** returns `io.EOF` -- distinct from a syntax error, and often means the client simply forgot to send a body at all rather than sending a malformed one.

```go
var req CreateUserRequest
err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req)
switch {
case errors.Is(err, io.EOF):
	http.Error(w, "request body is empty", http.StatusBadRequest)
	return
case err != nil:
	http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("invalid JSON: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
	return
}
```

All of these still warrant a `4xx` status -- they're the client's fault, not the server's -- but distinguishing them, even just in the message text returned to the caller, turns a generic 'something is wrong with your request' into something a client-side developer can act on immediately without guessing. It's also worth noting explicitly what `Decode` does **not** treat as an error by default: JSON fields with no matching struct field are silently ignored (matched case-insensitively against field names or tags, and simply dropped if nothing matches) -- unless the decoder is explicitly configured with `DisallowUnknownFields()`, forgetting an expected field's tag, or a client sending an unexpected extra field, will not by itself cause `Decode` to fail.

examples.title: Decoding a Request Body Into a Struct
examples.explanation: `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req)` streams directly from the request's body reader into `req`, populating `Name` and `Age` from whatever JSON keys match their tags (`"name"` and `"age"`). Note the deliberate order in the success path: `w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)` is called explicitly, before `Encode` gets a chance to implicitly send `200 OK` as its own first write -- this is the pattern for any handler that needs a non-200 success status (here, 201 Created, conventional for a successful resource-creation endpoint) alongside a JSON body. Setting `Content-Type` before `WriteHeader` (which itself must come before `Encode`'s first byte) keeps every header change safely ahead of anything that would lock the response in.

examples.title: Struct Tags in Action: omitempty and Unexported Fields
examples.explanation: `Nickname` is present in the struct but omitted from the output entirely, because it's tagged `omitempty` and its value is the empty string, the zero value for `string`. `password`, despite carrying a `json:"password"` tag that looks like it should include it under the key `"password"`, is never included at all -- because `password` starts with a lowercase letter, it's unexported, and encoding/json (operating via reflection, with no special access beyond what any other package would have) simply cannot read it, so the tag on an unreachable field is inert. This is a common trap: someone reviewing this struct's tags alone might reasonably assume `password` gets serialized under `"password"`, when in fact it's guaranteed to never appear in the output no matter what value it holds -- the capitalization of the field name, not the tag, decides visibility here.

examples.title: Distinguishing Decode Error Cases
examples.code:
package main

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net/http"
)

type Order struct {
	Quantity int `json:"quantity"`
}

func createOrderHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	var order Order
	err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&order)

	var typeErr *json.UnmarshalTypeError
	switch {
	case errors.Is(err, io.EOF):
		http.Error(w, "request body must not be empty", http.StatusBadRequest)
		return
	case errors.As(err, &typeErr):
		http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("field %q must be a %s", typeErr.Field, typeErr.Type), http.StatusBadRequest)
		return
	case err != nil:
		http.Error(w, "malformed JSON in request body", http.StatusBadRequest)
		return
	}

	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(order)
}
examples.explanation: `errors.Is(err, io.EOF)` specifically catches a genuinely empty body, giving the client a message that points at the actual problem (nothing was sent) rather than a generic parse failure. `errors.As(err, &typeErr)` checks whether the underlying error is specifically a `*json.UnmarshalTypeError` -- if the client sent `{"quantity": "five"}` (a string where an int is expected), this branch fires and can report exactly which field and expected type caused the failure, using information the error value itself carries. Any other non-nil error -- malformed syntax being the most common -- falls through to a generic 'malformed JSON' message. All three branches return a 400 Bad Request, correctly signaling client error in every case, but the message text differs meaningfully, giving whoever is debugging the client-side integration a genuinely useful starting point instead of one indistinguishable catch-all message.

misconceptions.description: A struct field needs a json tag in order to be included in the output when the struct is marshaled to JSON -- without one, encoding/json has no way to know what to do with it.
misconceptions.clarification: Exported fields are included in marshaled JSON by default, using the Go field's own name verbatim as the JSON key, with no tag required at all. A json tag is only needed to change that default behavior -- renaming the key, adding omitempty, or excluding the field entirely with "-" -- not to opt a field into being included in the first place. The one thing that genuinely determines whether a field can be included at all is whether it's exported (capitalized): unexported fields are always excluded from JSON output regardless of whether they carry a tag.

misconceptions.description: Any error returned from json.Decode means the client sent an empty or disconnected request, so it's safe to treat every decode error identically with one generic error response.
misconceptions.clarification: Decode can fail for several distinct and genuinely different reasons: a truly empty body (io.EOF), syntactically malformed JSON (a *json.SyntaxError), or a value whose JSON type doesn't match the target Go field's type (a *json.UnmarshalTypeError, which even names the offending field). Collapsing all of these into one identical, generic error message discards information the error value already carries -- information that, surfaced back to the caller, would let them fix a malformed request far faster than a single undifferentiated 'bad request' response would.

exercises.prompt: Given this struct and this value, what exact JSON string does json.Marshal produce?
exercises.code:
type Item struct {
	Title       string `json:"title"`
	Description string `json:"description,omitempty"`
	Quantity    int    `json:"quantity,omitempty"`
	internalID  string `json:"internal_id"`
}

item := Item{
	Title:       "Widget",
	Description: "",
	Quantity:    0,
	internalID:  "abc-123",
}
data, _ := json.Marshal(item)
fmt.Println(string(data))
hints: Title has no omitempty and a non-zero value, so it's always included under its tagged key.
Description and Quantity are both tagged omitempty and both currently hold their zero values ("" and 0) -- what does omitempty do to a field in exactly that state?
internalID starts with a lowercase letter -- does its json tag matter at all, regardless of what value it holds?
exercises.expectedAnswer: {"title":"Widget"} -- Description and Quantity are both omitted because they're tagged omitempty and hold their zero values. internalID is omitted entirely because it's unexported (lowercase), regardless of its json tag or its non-empty value "abc-123" -- encoding/json cannot see unexported fields at all.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Title is exported, has no omitempty, and holds the non-zero value "Widget", so it's included as {"title":"Widget"} unconditionally. Description is exported and tagged omitempty, and its current value is "" (the zero value for string), so it's dropped from the output entirely. Quantity is exported and tagged omitempty, and its current value is 0 (the zero value for int), so it's also dropped. internalID starts with a lowercase letter, making it unexported -- encoding/json, which operates via reflection with no special access privileges, cannot read unexported fields under any circumstances, so its json:"internal_id" tag is completely inert and it never appears in the output no matter what value it holds. The final marshaled result contains only the one field that is both exported and either untagged-with-omitempty or non-zero: {"title":"Widget"}.

exercises.prompt: This handler is supposed to return a JSON response with the correct Content-Type header, but clients report receiving a response with no Content-Type header set at all (or an incorrect default one, depending on the client). Find and fix the bug.
hints: Look at the order of the two lines: which one actually sends bytes to the client first?
Encode writes body bytes, and if no status/headers have been sent yet, that first write implicitly locks in the response's headers (with a default Content-Type) right then and there.
Once headers are sent, a later call to w.Header().Set(...) modifies a header map that has already been flushed -- it has no effect on what the client receives. Reorder the two lines.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code calls Encode first, which performs its first internal Write call immediately -- and because no status code or headers had been explicitly sent yet at that point, Go's net/http implicitly sends the response headers right then, using whatever Content-Type happened to be set in the header map at that exact moment (none, in the original code, since the Set call hadn't run yet). The subsequent w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json") call modifies the header map, but the headers have already been sent to the client by then, so this mutation has no effect on the actual response -- the client already received it, header-less (or with whatever default net/http applies). The fix simply reorders the two lines: set Content-Type first, so it's part of the header map by the time Encode's first Write triggers the implicit header send, and only then call Encode to write the actual JSON body.

assessments.prompt: A struct field is declared as `Count int` with no json tag at all. What happens when a value of that struct is marshaled to JSON?
options: The field is silently omitted, since only tagged fields are ever included in JSON output.
Marshaling fails with an error, since encoding/json requires every field to have an explicit tag.
The field is included in the output using the exact Go field name, "Count", as the JSON key, since exported fields are included by default with no tag required.
The field is included, but only if its value is non-zero -- untagged fields behave as if they had an implicit omitempty.
assessments.explanation: Exported fields (capitalized, like Count) are included in marshaled JSON by default, using the field's own Go name verbatim as the JSON key, with absolutely no tag required to achieve this -- a tag is only needed to change that default behavior (rename the key, add omitempty, or exclude the field with "-"). Option A and B are both wrong because they assume a tag is required for inclusion at all, which is backwards -- untagged exported fields are included, not excluded or erroring. Option D is wrong -- there is no implicit omitempty behavior for untagged fields; a zero-value untagged field is still included in the output (e.g. "Count":0), which is precisely why omitempty has to be added explicitly whenever that default inclusion-of-zero-values isn't wanted.

assessments.prompt: Walk through everything that can go wrong when decoding a JSON request body in an HTTP handler, and explain how to respond appropriately to each distinct case rather than collapsing them into one generic error response.
assessments.modelAnswer: A call to json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&target) can fail in at least three meaningfully different ways, and each deserves its own handling rather than one undifferentiated 'bad request' response. First, the request body might be genuinely empty -- the client sent no JSON at all -- which Decode reports as io.EOF; checking for this specifically with errors.Is(err, io.EOF) lets you tell the caller directly that a body was expected but none arrived, rather than implying their JSON was malformed when in fact none was sent. Second, the body might contain syntactically invalid JSON -- unbalanced braces, a trailing comma, an unquoted key -- which surfaces as a *json.SyntaxError; this genuinely is a parsing failure, and reporting it as such (optionally including the error's own message, which names the byte offset where parsing failed) gives a client-side developer something concrete to check. Third, the JSON might be syntactically valid but contain a value whose type doesn't match what the target struct field expects -- a string where a number belongs, for instance -- which produces a *json.UnmarshalTypeError; unlike a generic syntax error, this error value specifically names the offending field and the expected type, information worth surfacing directly in the response rather than discarding by treating it identically to a syntax error. All three cases warrant a 4xx status code, typically 400 Bad Request, since in every case the fault lies with the client's request rather than the server -- the distinction that matters is in the message returned, not the status class. It's also worth remembering what does NOT produce a decode error at all by default: JSON containing extra fields the target struct doesn't define are silently ignored rather than rejected, unless the decoder is explicitly configured with DisallowUnknownFields; a handler that needs to reject unexpected extra fields as a validation rule has to opt into that behavior explicitly rather than assuming Decode already enforces it.

concepts.title: The Middleware Pattern
concepts.description: Middleware in Go is simply a function that accepts an http.Handler and returns a new http.Handler wrapping it -- a direct, practical payoff of the small-interface Handler design that lets logging, authentication, and other cross-cutting concerns be composed around a handler without that handler ever needing to know they exist.
learningObjectives: Explain what the middleware pattern is and why it separates cross-cutting concerns like logging and authentication from a handler's own business logic.
Write a middleware function with signature func(http.Handler) http.Handler that wraps a handler with logging behavior around the call to the wrapped handler.
Chain multiple middleware functions together in a deliberate order, and explain how that order changes observable behavior.
Use context.Context with an unexported key type to pass a request-scoped value (such as an authenticated user) from middleware into a downstream handler safely.
Explain why middleware that rejects a request (such as failed authentication) must return immediately after writing its response, rather than falling through to call the wrapped handler.

sections.heading: What Middleware Is, and Why It Exists
sections.body:
Real HTTP services need the same handful of behaviors around nearly every request -- logging that a request happened, checking that the caller is authenticated, recovering from a panic so one bad request doesn't take down the whole server, timing how long a request took. Writing all of that directly inside every single handler duplicates it endlessly and, worse, ties unrelated concerns (is this user allowed to do this? vs. what does this specific endpoint actually do?) together in one function body, making both harder to read, test, and change independently.

**Middleware** solves this by wrapping a handler in another handler that runs some behavior, then calls the original, then optionally runs more behavior, all without the original handler ever being aware it's wrapped:

```go
type Middleware func(http.Handler) http.Handler
```

A middleware is a function that takes an `http.Handler` (the "next" handler in the chain) and returns a brand new `http.Handler` that wraps it. This is possible, cleanly, specifically because `http.Handler` is such a small interface -- exactly one method -- so "wrap a Handler" only ever means "produce something else with that same one method," regardless of how many layers deep the wrapping goes or what concrete type sits at the very center.

examples.title: A Standalone Logging Middleware
examples.explanation: `LoggingMiddleware(mux)` wraps the entire mux -- not one specific route -- in a single logging layer, which is a common, deliberate choice: applying middleware around the whole mux logs every route uniformly, in one place, rather than requiring every individual `HandleFunc` call to separately opt into logging. `wrapped` has type `http.Handler` (specifically, the `http.HandlerFunc` that `LoggingMiddleware` returned), and it's passed directly to `http.ListenAndServe` exactly where `mux` itself would have gone -- from `ListenAndServe`'s point of view, there's no observable difference between being handed a bare mux and being handed a mux wrapped in an arbitrary number of middleware layers, which is precisely the point of the pattern.

examples.title: Chaining Multiple Middleware in a Deliberate Order
examples.explanation: `Chain` applies its middlewares in reverse order internally (`mws[len(mws)-1]` first) specifically so that the resulting call order matches the order the middlewares are *listed* in at the call site -- `Chain(mux, RecoverMiddleware, LoggingMiddleware, AuthMiddleware)` produces a handler where `RecoverMiddleware` runs outermost (first to see every request, including ones that later panic), `LoggingMiddleware` runs next (logging every request that gets this far, including ones Auth will go on to reject), and `AuthMiddleware` runs innermost, immediately before the actual mux. Putting `RecoverMiddleware` outermost is itself a deliberate, common convention: if any inner middleware or handler panics, only a layer that wraps *everything* below it can reliably catch that panic via a deferred `recover()` and turn it into a clean 500 response instead of crashing the entire server process.

examples.title: Auth Middleware Passing a User via context.Context
examples.explanation: The unexported `contextKey` type and its single constant `userContextKey` guarantee this key can never collide with a context key defined in any other package, even one that happens to store its own value under a plain string like "user" or under an int with the same underlying value -- Go's type system treats `contextKey(0)` as a distinct type from a bare `int` or `string`, so only code inside this package (or code explicitly given this exact constant) can ever produce a matching key. The explicit `return` after `http.Error` is what actually enforces the auth check -- without it, `next.ServeHTTP` would run regardless of whether `ok` was true or false. `profileHandler`'s type-asserted retrieval, `r.Context().Value(userContextKey).(User)`, only ever succeeds because `AuthMiddleware` is guaranteed to run before it in the chain and guaranteed to have already returned early on any request that didn't pass authentication.

misconceptions.description: Using a plain string like "user" as the key argument to context.WithValue and context.Value is a harmless, common convenience, since context keys are just meant to be simple lookup labels.
misconceptions.clarification: A plain string (or any built-in type like int) used directly as a context key creates a real collision risk across unrelated packages: any other code -- including a third-party middleware you don't control -- could use that exact same string value as its own context key, and the two would silently read and overwrite each other's stored value with no compiler warning, since context.Context stores values in a way that's only distinguished by the key's type and value together. The idiomatic fix is to define a small, unexported named type specific to your own package (commonly a tiny int-based type) and use a constant of that type as the key -- since no other package can construct a value of an unexported type it doesn't define, this guarantees the key can never collide with any other package's context key, no matter what underlying value either happens to use.

misconceptions.description: If a middleware writes an error status and message to the ResponseWriter (for example via http.Error) inside an if block, execution automatically stops there -- there's no need to add an explicit return statement afterward.
misconceptions.clarification: Writing to an http.ResponseWriter is an ordinary function call with no special control-flow effect on the surrounding Go code -- it does not cause the function to return, panic, or otherwise stop executing subsequent statements. Without an explicit `return` immediately after the error response, execution falls through to whatever comes next in the function, which in middleware typically means calling next.ServeHTTP(w, r) regardless of whether the preceding check actually passed or failed -- letting the wrapped handler run its real logic even for a request that was supposed to be rejected. This is a genuinely common, easy-to-introduce bug precisely because the code compiles without any warning and can pass casual manual testing whenever the happy path (successful auth) is what gets tested.

exercises.prompt: Given this middleware chain and handler, in what exact order do the four print statements execute when a single request comes in?
hints: Read the wrapping from the outside in to find the order execution ENTERS each layer: MiddlewareA wraps MiddlewareB, which wraps finalHandler.
Each middleware's 'before' print happens before it calls next.ServeHTTP, and its 'after' print happens once next.ServeHTTP has fully returned.
Think of it like nested parentheses or an onion: the outermost layer's 'before' runs first, and its 'after' runs LAST, once everything inside it has completely finished.
exercises.expectedAnswer: A: before, B: before, final handler, B: after, A: after -- in that exact order. Execution enters the outermost middleware (A) first, then the next layer in (B), then the innermost handler, and then unwinds back out in the reverse order, with each layer's 'after' print firing only once everything it wrapped has fully completed.
exercises.solutionExplanation: handler is MiddlewareA wrapping (MiddlewareB wrapping finalHandler), so calling handler.ServeHTTP first runs MiddlewareA's body: it prints 'A: before', then calls next.ServeHTTP, which is MiddlewareB's ServeHTTP. That prints 'B: before', then calls ITS next.ServeHTTP, which is finalHandler, printing 'final handler' and returning immediately (it has no next to call). Control now unwinds back into MiddlewareB's function, past its next.ServeHTTP call, which prints 'B: after' and returns. Control unwinds one more level, back into MiddlewareA's function, past ITS next.ServeHTTP call, which prints 'A: after' and finally returns to whatever called handler.ServeHTTP in the first place. The result is a strict nested ordering -- 'before' prints happen in outside-to-inside order, and 'after' prints happen in the exact reverse, inside-to-outside order, mirroring how nested function calls unwind.

exercises.prompt: This auth middleware is supposed to block any request without a valid API key, responding with 401 and never running the wrapped handler for rejected requests. Instead, testers report that even requests with a missing or wrong API key still seem to trigger the wrapped handler's real behavior (visible via its own log lines), alongside the 401 response. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Writing to the ResponseWriter with http.Error does not, by itself, stop the enclosing function from continuing to its next statement.
Trace execution when key != validAPIKey is true: http.Error runs, and then what's the very next line the function executes?
Add an explicit return statement immediately after the http.Error call, inside the if block, so next.ServeHTTP is never reached for a rejected request.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code calls http.Error to write a 401 response when the API key check fails, but has no return statement inside that if block -- so regardless of whether the key was valid, execution always falls through to the unconditional next.ServeHTTP(w, r) call directly below the if statement. This means a rejected request still gets the wrapped handler's real logic executed against it (explaining the wrapped handler's own log lines appearing even for invalid-key requests), in addition to the 401 response already sent -- and if the wrapped handler itself tries to write its own status code or body, that produces a 'superfluous response.WriteHeader call' warning on top of the underlying security bug of running privileged logic for an unauthenticated request. Adding `return` immediately after the http.Error call ensures that when the key check fails, the function exits right there, and next.ServeHTTP is never reached at all for a rejected request -- exactly matching the intended behavior of blocking access entirely.

assessments.prompt: Given `handler := LoggingMiddleware(AuthMiddleware(finalHandler))`, which statement correctly describes the order requests and responses flow through these three pieces?
options: Requests flow finalHandler -> AuthMiddleware -> LoggingMiddleware, and responses flow back in the same order.

Requests flow LoggingMiddleware -> AuthMiddleware -> finalHandler; the response then unwinds back through AuthMiddleware and LoggingMiddleware in reverse, so LoggingMiddleware's own post-call code (such as a timing log) runs last, after everything else has completed.
All three run simultaneously in separate goroutines, so there is no defined ordering between them.
LoggingMiddleware and AuthMiddleware both run before the request even reaches finalHandler, but which of the two runs first is undefined and decided randomly by the Go runtime.
assessments.explanation: LoggingMiddleware is the outermost wrapper (it's the function call surrounding everything else), so its body starts executing first when a request arrives -- it then calls into AuthMiddleware, which in turn calls into finalHandler if authentication succeeds. Once finalHandler returns, control unwinds back through AuthMiddleware's remaining code (if any), and finally back through LoggingMiddleware's remaining code (its timing log, typically), which is why that log line reflects the total time including everything nested inside it. Option A describes the reverse order, which is wrong. Option C is wrong -- middleware wrapping is synchronous, sequential function calls, not concurrent goroutines, unless a middleware explicitly spawns one itself. Option D is wrong -- the order is entirely deterministic and directly determined by the nesting shown in the wrapping expression itself, not randomized.

assessments.prompt: Explain the middleware pattern to a developer who understands http.Handler but has never written or read middleware before, and explain specifically why forgetting a return statement after a short-circuiting error response is such a common and dangerous mistake in this pattern.
assessments.modelAnswer: Middleware is a function that takes an http.Handler and returns a new http.Handler that wraps it -- typically by running some behavior, then calling the original wrapped handler's ServeHTTP method to let it do its real work, and then optionally running more behavior once that call returns. This is only possible so cleanly because http.Handler is a tiny, one-method interface: 'wrap a handler' always just means 'produce another thing with that same one ServeHTTP method,' so middleware can be stacked arbitrarily deep, and neither the mux registering the final wrapped result nor any individual layer needs to know or care how many other layers are involved, or what the innermost handler actually does. This is exactly how you get to separate cross-cutting concerns -- logging every request, checking authentication, recovering from panics -- from each individual handler's own business logic: the handler itself stays focused purely on its own job, while behavior that should apply uniformly across many or all handlers gets written exactly once, as a wrapping layer, and applied by composing it around whatever it needs to wrap. The return-statement danger is specific to middleware that's meant to short-circuit a request -- reject it outright, most commonly for failed authentication -- before it ever reaches the wrapped handler. Writing an error response with something like http.Error(w, ...) is just an ordinary function call in Go; it has no special effect on the enclosing function's control flow, so unless that call is immediately followed by an explicit return, execution simply continues on to whatever's written next, which in nearly every middleware is the unconditional call to next.ServeHTTP(w, r). Forgetting the return therefore means the middleware still writes its rejection response, but then goes on to run the wrapped handler's real logic anyway, regardless of whether the check that was supposed to gate access actually passed. This is dangerous specifically because it's silent and easy to miss: the code compiles without any error or warning, a request that happens to pass the check during casual testing behaves identically whether the return is there or not, and the bug only becomes visible on a request that should have been rejected -- exactly the case a developer is least likely to test carefully, since it's the 'unhappy' path rather than the one they're actively building and exercising.
